title: N6OL Powerline QRM Monitor configuration
description: Every setting the monitor reads. Each section is one table of ~/.buzz/config.toml.

audio.title: Audio input
audio.description: Where live audio comes from, and what the analyzer expects of it.

source.title: Audio source
source.description: Where live audio comes from: a radio feeding a sound card, or one of the receivers this program drives.

x-enum-titles.soundcard: Sound card - a radio in SSB, wired to an audio input
x-enum-titles.rtlsdr: RTL-SDR - a receiver, set up in the RTL-SDR section
x-enum-titles.sdrplay: SDRplay - an RSP1A or RSP1B, set up in the SDRplay section

input_device_name.title: Input device
input_device_name.description: The sound card that carries the RF-to-audio converted signal.
input_device_name.x-sample-commented: Whatever Setup finds on your machine. The value shown names one sound card and is only an example.
x-notes: Choose this in Setup's Audio step. Do not type it. Setup probes every input, shows a level bar for each, and writes the name for you.
The monitor finds the device by this name at every start. It never uses a stored index. Names survive a reboot. Indices do not.

sample_rate.title: Sample rate (Hz)
sample_rate.description: The audio sample rate. It must match a rate the input device uses.
x-notes: The monitor enforces this band. It does not treat it as advice.
Below 8000 Hz the 4 kHz that the waterfall and the analysis look at sits above Nyquist. Nothing is there to measure.
Above 48000 Hz the ring buffer is a fixed size, so it holds too little history for the analyzer to acquire the way it was tuned. A powerline arc has nothing to say up there anyway.
16000 Hz is enough for this measurement and keeps CPU load low. That matters for a monitor that runs all day without an operator.

pulse_rate.title: Pulse rate (pps)
pulse_rate.description: Impulses per second from the mains. This is twice the grid frequency, because an arc fires on both peaks.

x-enum-titles.100: 100 pps - 50 Hz grid (Europe and most other places)

rtlsdr.title: RTL-SDR receiver
rtlsdr.description: Settings for an RTL-SDR receiver. Used only when the audio source is set to RTL-SDR.

frequency_khz.title: Listening frequency (kHz)
frequency_khz.description: The frequency to listen on. The receiver tunes 50 kHz above it and the difference is undone in software, so this is the frequency that gets measured.
x-notes: In kHz, so 80m is around 3588 and 40m around 7074. Tenths are allowed if you want a frequency to the nearest hundred Hz.
The default puts the whole 256 kHz the receiver samples inside 80m and clear of the CW DX window. Powerline noise is generally worse low in HF.

gain_db.title: Tuner gain (dB)
gain_db.description: The monitor snaps this to the nearest step the tuner offers, since the tuner accepts only a fixed set.
x-notes: Choose the lowest gain at which band noise just overtakes the receiver's own noise. An 8-bit receiver cannot afford more than that, because the room an arc needs takes most of its range, so the noise floor it reports reads about 3 dB high. Lower leaves more room for loud events. Higher measures the receiver rather than the band.

calibrated_offset_db.title: Level calibration (dB)
calibrated_offset_db.description: The offset that converts audio amplitude to RF level at the receiver input, the same job [station] audio_rf_conversion_db does for a sound card. Leave it unset until you have calibrated.
x-notes: This replaces [station] audio_rf_conversion_db whenever [audio] source is rtlsdr. The two carry different names because they are different quantities: that one describes a radio and its wiring, this one is mostly the negative of the tuner gain above and moves whenever the gain does.
Unset means the monitor estimates it as the negative of the tuner gain. Expect the reading to be a few dB out. The [station] figure is not a fallback and is never used for a receiver.

To find the figure, read the noise floor on a radio you trust, on the same antenna at the same time, with its filter set to match the bandwidth above. The difference between the two readings is what goes here.
It depends on the tuner gain, so changing that means finding it again.

calibrated_at_gain_db.title: Calibrated at gain (dB)
calibrated_at_gain_db.description: The tuner gain the level calibration was measured against. The calibration tool writes this, and nobody sets it by hand.
x-notes: The calibration tool writes this when it measures the level calibration above.
Change the tuner gain afterwards and the calibration is wrong by roughly the difference, so startup compares the two and says so. Run the calibration again rather than editing this.

arc_headroom_db.title: Arc headroom (dB)
arc_headroom_db.description: Room the gain calibration keeps above the quiet band noise, so that an arc has somewhere to go before it clips.
x-notes: This value comes from measurement rather than choice. Over 11147 locked minutes at one station the loudest arc reached 30.95 dB above its own noise floor, and nothing reached 35. The extra covers the wider bandwidth the receiver clips across.
Raising it lowers the gain the calibration will pick, so more of the reported noise floor becomes the receiver's own rather than the band's.

device_index.title: Receiver number
device_index.description: Which receiver to use when more than one is plugged in.

iq_sample_rate.title: Receiver sample rate (Hz)
iq_sample_rate.description: How fast the receiver samples. It must divide evenly by the decimation below.
x-notes: 256000 divided by 16 gives 16000 Hz of audio, the rate a sound-card station uses.
The receiver rate divided by the decimation has to come to between 8000 Hz and 48000 Hz. A receiver rate of 2400000 needs a decimation between 50 and 300.

decimation.title: Decimation
decimation.description: Receiver samples per audio sample. The audio rate is the receiver rate divided by this.

bandwidth_khz.title: Bandwidth (kHz)
bandwidth_khz.description: How much of the band to measure, on one side of the listening frequency.
x-notes: 4 kHz matches a typical SSB filter, so levels compare with a radio tuned to the same spot.

At most the receiver rate divided by the decimation, divided again by 2.5. That is 6.4 kHz with the settings above. The filter needs the extra room past the band edge, and the monitor refuses a wider setting and says what the limit is.

tuning_offset_khz.title: Tuning offset (kHz)
tuning_offset_khz.description: How far from the listening frequency to tune the hardware. Undone in software, so it changes nothing you measure.
x-notes: The receiver puts a false signal at its own tuning frequency, and this moves that away from the measured band. Leave it alone unless you know why you are changing it.

sideband.title: Sideband
sideband.description: Which side of the listening frequency to hear.

x-enum-titles.upper: Upper - the spectrum above the listening frequency
x-enum-titles.lower: Lower - the spectrum below it, shown reversed

sdrplay.title: SDRplay receiver
sdrplay.description: Settings for an SDRplay RSP1A or RSP1B. Used only when the audio source is set to SDRplay.

frequency_khz.title: Listening frequency (kHz)
frequency_khz.description: The frequency to listen on. The receiver tunes 50 kHz above it and the difference is undone in software, so this is the frequency that gets measured.
x-notes: In kHz, so 80m is around 3588 and 40m around 7074. Tenths are allowed if you want a frequency to the nearest hundred Hz.
The default puts the whole 256 kHz the receiver samples inside 80m and clear of the CW DX window. Powerline noise is generally worse low in HF.

gain_db.title: Receiver gain (dB)
gain_db.description: The monitor snaps this to the nearest whole decibel the receiver reaches, from -29 to 71.
x-notes: An RSP is set in gain reduction rather than in gain, and this states it as gain anyway, so that it means the same thing here as it does for an RTL-SDR.

Choose the lowest gain at which band noise sits about 10 dB above the receiver's own noise. A 14-bit receiver has the range for that, so the noise floor it reports reads well under a decibel high, where an 8-bit one has to settle for about 3 dB. Automatic gain selection aims at the same place, and the headroom and overload limits still take priority. Lower leaves more room for loud events. Higher measures the receiver rather than the band.

calibrated_offset_db.title: Level calibration (dB)
calibrated_offset_db.description: The offset that converts audio amplitude to RF level at the receiver input, the same job [station] audio_rf_conversion_db does for a sound card. Leave it unset until you have calibrated.
x-notes: This replaces [station] audio_rf_conversion_db whenever [audio] source is sdrplay. The two carry different names because they are different quantities: that one describes a radio and its wiring, this one is mostly the negative of the gain above and moves whenever the gain does.

Unset means the monitor estimates it as 11 dB minus the receiver gain. The 11 dB fixed conversion estimate came from one RSP1B above its noise-floor knee, so expect another unit to differ. The [station] figure is not a fallback and is never used for a receiver.

To find the figure, read the noise floor on a radio you trust, on the same antenna at the same time, with its filter set to match the bandwidth above. The difference between the two readings is what goes here.
It depends on the receiver gain, so changing that means finding it again.

calibrated_at_gain_db.title: Calibrated at gain (dB)
calibrated_at_gain_db.description: The receiver gain the level calibration was measured against. The calibration tool writes this, and nobody sets it by hand.
x-notes: The calibration tool writes this when it measures the level calibration above.
Change the receiver gain afterwards and the calibration is wrong by roughly the difference, so startup compares the two and says so. Run the calibration again rather than editing this.

arc_headroom_db.title: Arc headroom (dB)
arc_headroom_db.description: Room the gain calibration keeps above the quiet band noise, so that an arc has somewhere to go before it clips.
x-notes: This value comes from measurement rather than choice. Over 11147 locked minutes at one station the loudest arc reached 30.95 dB above its own noise floor, and nothing reached 35. The extra covers the wider bandwidth the receiver clips across.
Raising it lowers the gain the calibration will pick, so more of the reported noise floor becomes the receiver's own rather than the band's.

device_index.title: Receiver number
device_index.description: Which receiver to use when more than one RSP is plugged in.

iq_sample_rate.title: Receiver sample rate (Hz)
iq_sample_rate.description: How fast the receiver samples. It must divide evenly by the decimation below.
x-notes: 256000 divided by 16 gives 16000 Hz of audio, the rate a sound-card station uses.
The receiver rate divided by the decimation has to come to between 8000 Hz and 48000 Hz. A receiver rate of 2400000 needs a decimation between 50 and 300.

decimation.title: Decimation
decimation.description: Receiver samples per audio sample. The audio rate is the receiver rate divided by this.

bandwidth_khz.title: Bandwidth (kHz)
bandwidth_khz.description: How much of the band to measure, on one side of the listening frequency.
x-notes: 4 kHz matches a typical SSB filter, so levels compare with a radio tuned to the same spot.

At most the receiver rate divided by the decimation, divided again by 2.5. That is 6.4 kHz with the settings above. The filter needs the extra room past the band edge, and the monitor refuses a wider setting and says what the limit is.

tuning_offset_khz.title: Tuning offset (kHz)
tuning_offset_khz.description: How far from the listening frequency to tune the hardware. Undone in software, so it changes nothing you measure.
x-notes: A receiver puts a strong false signal at exactly its own tuning frequency, and this moves that out of the measured band. The monitor undoes it in software.

sideband.title: Sideband
sideband.description: Which side of the listening frequency to hear.

x-enum-titles.upper: Upper - the spectrum above the listening frequency
x-enum-titles.lower: Lower - the spectrum below it, shown reversed

api_path.title: SDRplay API library path
api_path.description: Where the SDRplay API library is, for an installation the monitor cannot find on its own. Leave it unset to search.
x-notes: Unset means the monitor tries the plain library name first, so an installation already on the search path wins, then the directories an installer uses.

station.title: Station
station.description: Who measures, from where, and the calibration that turns audio into dBm.

callsign.title: Callsign
callsign.description: Your amateur radio callsign. It appears in page titles and plot labels.

timezone.title: Timezone
timezone.description: The IANA timezone name for CSV timestamps and graph labels, such as America/Los_Angeles.

path.title: Output directory
path.description: Where the monitor writes CSV files, plots, and the index page.
path.x-default-from-runtime: Your home directory, resolved when the program starts.
x-notes: Recordings go to a 'recordings' folder under this path, unless the recording section names a directory of its own.

noise_floor.title: Receiver noise floor (dBm)
noise_floor.description: The baseline for the noise-floor reference line on the daily graph.
x-notes: You may want to adjust this after gathering a few days of data, to see what is typical for your area in the absence of any utility noise.

noise_min_snr.title: Minimum SNR for a detection (dB)
noise_min_snr.description: How far above the noise floor a reading must sit to count as interference in the probability summaries.

audio_rf_conversion_db.title: Audio-to-RF offset (dB)
audio_rf_conversion_db.description: The offset that converts audio amplitude to RF level at the receiver input. This one is for a sound card. A receiver uses calibrated_offset_db in its own section instead and ignores this.
x-notes: Two settings share this name, and exactly one applies. With [audio] source set to soundcard, this is the one in use. With it set to rtlsdr, the monitor replaces this at startup with the receiver's own figure, so editing it there changes nothing.

This number is added to the audio level to approximate the RF level in dBm at the receiver input.  For example, if your radio's own S-meter reads -64 dBm and the sound card sees -32 dB of audio for that same signal, set this to -32.
Most receivers: leave this alone.  Open the Calibration meter on the Audio page instead, and adjust the RF and AF gain on the receiver until its own S-meter agrees with the reading there.

Some receivers have no AF gain to adjust - one with its own internal sound device, for instance. Choose this field itself to open a live meter of its own: Up and Down move the offset by 0.1 dB, PageUp and PageDown by 1 dB, Space resets it to the default, and Enter confirms.
S9 is -73 dBm, and each S-unit is 6 dB.
Set the radio up for measurement first: AGC off, widest filter, SSB, preamp and attenuator off. Tune where the antenna is resonant and bypass the tuner.

enable_all_time_summary.title: All-time summary graph
enable_all_time_summary.description: Publish a probability summary covering your whole data set, alongside the 7-day and 30-day ones.
x-notes: The 7-day and 30-day summaries are always published. This adds a third chart, averaging every day since summary_start_date_iso.
Leave it off if your noise has changed since that date.

summary_start_date_iso.title: Summary graph start date
summary_start_date_iso.description: The ISO 8601 date that the all-time probability summary graph starts from. It applies only when that graph is turned on.

enable_frequency_chart.title: Grid frequency chart
enable_frequency_chart.description: Publish a chart of the estimated grid frequency over the current day.
x-notes: One chart, current_frequency_estimate.png, covering today only and overwritten each minute. It runs from midnight to the moment it was drawn.
Minutes with no lock on the pulse train are left blank rather than joined up.
Your hardware's sampling clock is never exactly its nominal rate, and that scales the reading. Read the chart for how the frequency moves rather than for what it is.

weather.title: Weather
weather.description: Weather readings logged beside each measurement. Arcing often follows humidity and wind.

source.title: Weather source
source.description: Where weather readings come from. Choose none to leave those CSV columns empty.

x-enum-titles.cumulusmx: CumulusMX - a weather station on your own network
x-enum-titles.openmeteo: Open-Meteo - a free public API that needs no account
x-enum-titles.none: None - leave the weather columns empty

url.title: CumulusMX endpoint
url.description: The JSON endpoint of your CumulusMX installation.
x-notes: Change the query string tags to match the fields your station publishes.
You should normally only change the hostname and port here.

latitude.title: Latitude
latitude.description: The latitude that Open-Meteo looks up.
x-notes: The example is the Holmdel horn antenna in New Jersey, a National Historic Landmark, where Penzias and Wilson spent a year eliminating noise sources, pigeons included, before the hiss that was left turned out to be the cosmic microwave background.

longitude.title: Longitude
longitude.description: The longitude that Open-Meteo looks up.

then.comment: `required` alone would pass: both keys are present, holding null. Open-Meteo needs real coordinates, so the type has to narrow here too.

server.title: Web publishing
server.description: Upload plots and data to a web server over SCP, so anyone can see the results. This is off by default, and the monitor then runs on this machine alone.

enabled.title: Publish to a web server
enabled.description: Upload output files after each collection cycle. The monitor ignores every setting below while this is off.

host.title: Server hostname
host.description: The hostname or IP address of the web server that holds the published output.

username.title: SSH username
username.description: The account to log in as on that server.

remote_path.title: Remote path
remote_path.description: Where uploaded files go on the server. End it with a slash.

key_path.title: SSH private key
key_path.description: The private key that authenticates the upload. It must have no passphrase, so uploads run without an operator.
key_path.x-default-from-runtime: buzz.pem inside the .buzz folder in your home directory.
x-notes: Generate one with: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.buzz/buzz.pem -N ""
Append ~/.buzz/buzz.pem.pub to the server account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Confirm that the key works before you switch uploads on.
On Windows, use forward slashes or double backslashes. TOML reads one backslash as the start of an escape sequence.

current_chart.title: Current chart link
current_chart.description: How the web page finds today's chart. The page reads one fixed address, data/current.png, so it never has to work out today's filename.

x-enum-titles.copy: Copy - upload the chart a second time under the fixed name
x-enum-titles.symlink: Symlink - point the fixed name at today's chart

x-notes: Copy works on every web server and needs no configuration. It uploads one extra chart per minute, around 85 kB.

Symlink saves that upload, but the web server has to follow symbolic links. Apache needs FollowSymLinks for the upload directory, and some shared hosts refuse to allow it. Nginx and lighttpd follow links by default.
If the page shows a broken image after you choose symlink, the server is not following the link. Switch back to copy.

recording.title: Event recording
recording.description: Save interference events as .wav files. Replay one later with --playback, or render it to video with --render.

enabled.title: Arm recording at startup
enabled.description: Start with recording armed. The Record button, or the R key, toggles it while the monitor runs. The --enable-recording flag arms it for one run.
x-notes: A recording starts when the analyzer locks onto the pulse train. It ends once the signal has been gone for stop_after_seconds.

It opens with the audio the monitor had already buffered at the moment of the lock, and it ends with the silence it waited through. An event that starts and ends while the monitor runs is therefore captured whole, with a run-up and a run-out around it.

directory.title: Recording directory
directory.description: Where the monitor writes .wav files. Leave it empty to use a 'recordings' folder under the station output path.
directory.x-sample-commented: A 'recordings' folder under the station output path.
x-notes: The --playback flag also looks here when you give it a bare filename instead of a path.

min_free_disk_percent.title: Minimum free disk (%)
min_free_disk_percent.description: Percentage of the disk to leave free. Recording is held off while the disk is below this, and resumes on its own once there is room.
x-notes: Checked before each event rather than before each write, so being wrong about it costs at most one recording: max_seconds of it, which is about sixty megabytes of raw IQ at the default settings.
Set it to 0 to record until the disk is full.

max_events.title: Events to record
max_events.description: How many of the next events to capture before recording disarms itself. Set 0 to record every event until you switch recording off.

rearm_reset_minutes.title: Budget reset (minutes)
rearm_reset_minutes.description: How often to refill that budget, which makes it a rate instead of a one-off. 1440 gives max_events every day. Set 0 to never re-arm.
x-notes: The cycle runs from the last reset, not from the moment the budget ran out. It therefore keeps its time of day instead of sliding later by however long each day's events took to arrive.
A quiet period does not carry unused events forward. Switching recording off by hand also cancels the cycle.

max_seconds.title: Longest recording (seconds)
max_seconds.description: How much of the interference to record, measured from the lock. Set 0 to record the whole event however long it runs.
x-notes: This measures the event, not the file. The run-up that the ring buffer already held comes free on top, and so does the trailer afterward. The .wav on disk is therefore always longer than this.
A min_lock_seconds wait counts against this, because the monitor keeps those seconds and they are part of the event. Three seconds there and ten here give ten seconds of event, not thirteen.
A min_lock_snr wait does not count. That wait is open-ended, and charging it would spend the whole allowance before the file even opened.
Expect an overrun of up to 200 ms. The recorder polls rather than watching continuously.
A capped recording does not roll over into a second file. The monitor skips the rest of that event and starts the next file at the next event. The cap always wins over stop_after_seconds.

stop_after_seconds.title: Stop after silence (seconds)
stop_after_seconds.description: How many seconds without a lock end a recording. The monitor keeps this audio, so it also sets how much trailer every recording ends with.
x-notes: Raise it if one flickering signal splits across several files. Lower it to trim dead air off the end.

min_lock_seconds.title: Minimum lock before recording (seconds)
min_lock_seconds.description: How long the interference must hold before a recording starts. Set 0 to record every lock, however brief.
x-notes: A night of two-second blips otherwise fills the directory with files too short to replay.

Keep it to five seconds or less. The lead-in pays for it, because that audio comes from a sliding window a few seconds long. Wait two seconds and every recording opens two seconds later against the event.
The monitor clamps the value to the lower of the buffer length and max_seconds. It warns and says which one it used.

min_lock_snr.title: Minimum SNR before recording (dB)
min_lock_snr.description: How loud the interference must be before a recording starts. This keeps barely audible events off the disk.
x-notes: This affects recording alone. It does not change when the analyzer locks, measures, logs, or draws. That happens at a fixed 6 dB SNR in the code, so any value at or below 6 does nothing.
A signal that starts quiet and grows louder is not skipped. Recording starts the moment it crosses, so the monitor catches the event even when it misses the opening seconds.

The lead-in pays for the wait, and the lead-in runs out. This differs from min_lock_seconds, which the monitor can clamp: this wait depends on the signal rather than the clock. Something in the low teens is a reasonable place to start.

record_iq.title: Record raw IQ
record_iq.description: Write a second .wav of raw IQ beside each event recording, for handing the raw data to somebody who wants to process it themselves.
x-notes: The monitor keeps the last several seconds of raw IQ at all times when this is on, so that an IQ recording gets the same run-up its audio does. That is 4.7 MB at the default sample rate and 44 MB at the highest the hardware takes.
Nothing in this program reads an IQ recording back. Playing one is a job for other software.
An SDR receiver only. A sound card has no IQ to record, so the monitor ignores this and says so at startup when [audio] source is soundcard.

render.title: Video rendering
render.description: Where to find ffmpeg. Only --render and the loudness probe that feeds it need it. Only specify this if it cannot be found on the PATH.

ffmpeg_path.title: ffmpeg location
ffmpeg_path.description: Leave this empty to search PATH, where a normal install puts ffmpeg.
x-notes: Set it only when ffmpeg sits somewhere PATH does not reach. Two cases: a Windows build unzipped into a folder, and winget's shim directory in a terminal you have not restarted since the install.
Either the binary or the folder that holds it will do. A copy on PATH wins over this setting.
A monitor that never renders never looks for ffmpeg, so an empty value costs nothing.
